claim: Randall identifies the few zero-focalized (omniscient) passages as the mythic set pieces perceived by no character, e.g. the Arthurian trio's departure.
source: Neil Randall, 'Shifting Focalization and the Strategy of Delay: The Narrative Weaving of The Fionavar Tapestry', Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991), reprinted on Bright Weavings
quote: shifts to an unspecified focalizant, to omniscience

verdict.trueWording: perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim: 'The departure of the Arthurian trio is one of several brief passages in the trilogy that shifts to an unspecified focalizant, to omniscience, to what Genette calls zero focalization'. But the page says the OPPOSITE of 'perceived by no character' for this passage - 'The departure of the trio is more magnificent because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence' (and the text itself: 'it seemed to those that watched from the plain'). 'because in his case there are no observers' is said of Darien's death, which is strictly focalized, NOT zero-focalized. The 'mythic set pieces' limb is also weakened: Randall says the departure 'represents, of course, myth in the making, but for Fionavar the incident is less mythically significant than Darien's death.' Zero focalization means an UNSPECIFIED focalizant, not an unperceived event.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the zero-focalized passages are perceived by no character

claim: Kleander quotes Kay that the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium was written as a mosaic of different focalizations.
source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
quote: the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium was written as a mosaic

verdict.trueWording: Kay is quoted only for ‘written as a mosaic’
verdict.note: Raw page: "Kay's novels heavily rely on this technique, for example 'the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium was written as a mosaic' (Kay in New York Review of Science Fiction Interview 2000, url) of different focalizations." The quotation marks CLOSE after 'a mosaic' and the citation follows; 'of different focalizations' is Kleander's own completion of her sentence, not part of what she quotes from Kay. Kleander does assert the mosaic is of focalizations, but Kay must not be re-quoted as having said 'a mosaic of different focalizations'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Kay's quoted words include 'of different focalizations'

claim: Kleander reads Pertennius (Procopius) as Kay's illustration that history is carved and chosen, with the narrator's opening line that writers of history seek the dramatic over the truth.
source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)

verdict.trueWording: Pertennius sets out to ‘choose, sever and carve’ among events
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that 'writers of history seek the dramatic over the truth' is the narrator's opening line, and that Kleander attaches it to the Pertennius reading — the dissertation quotes 'seek the dramatic over the truth' (StS, 3) in a later, separate passage about Kay's own licence ('Being thus free to ‘seek the dramatic over the truth’ Kay teaches that there is no such thing as an ‘objective truth’'), never calls it an opening line or a narrator's line, and the word 'narrator' appears only twice on the page, both times about focalization theory
verdict.note: Quote 'exquisitely phrased vituperation' is verbatim ('depicts Crispin reading Pertennius’ ‘exquisitely phrased vituperation’ (LoE, 154)'). Supported limbs: Pertennius is 'Kay’s most obvious illustration of how ‘history can become dangerous when the creative aspect of its construction is concealed or unknown’'; 'Pertennius is modelled on Procopius'; 'As Pertennius sets out to ‘choose, sever and carve’ (White 1973, 288) among events'. Searched raw text for 'opening line', 'first line', 'writers of history': zero hits.

claim: Taylor documents that the Sarantine titles and vision derive from Yeats's Byzantium poems and that the title phrase is an in-world idiom for a life at a cusp.
source: Dena Taylor, 'On Sailing to Sarantium', TransVersions 10 (1999)

verdict.trueWording: The title refers to ... 'his life was on the cusp of change'; Kay drew Yeats's vision
verdict.note: Raw HTML fetched live (200) from brightweavings.com/denasailing/, 'by Dena Taylor', headnote 'first published as a review in TransVersions 10, Toronto: Orchid Press, 1999'. The quote 'Kay at his most historical' is on the page verbatim ('Here is Kay at his most historical'), and the idiom limb is fully supported verbatim: "To say of a man that he was sailing to Sarantium was to say that his life was on the cusp of change". The vision limb is supported ('what he has drawn from Yeats's vision of Byzantium'). But the page names exactly ONE Yeats poem, 'Sailing to Byzantium', never a plural set of Byzantium poems, and never states that any title DERIVES from Yeats - it attributes the title to the in-world idiom instead. (That derivation is asserted elsewhere, in Malosse's note 12, not in Taylor.) Graded PARTIAL on the plural/derivation limb.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the Sarantine titles derive from Yeats's Byzantium poems - the page names one poem ('Sailing to Byzantium'), discusses one title, and attributes only the VISION to Yeats, never the title's derivation

claim: Kay answers Henry James: treating the past as fantasy acknowledges the impossibility of recovering past world-views, a way of being honest about limitations.
source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away' (keynote essay; shorter version in The Globe and Mail, fall 1999) — Wayback copy of the Bright Weavings text
quote: a way of being honest about limitations

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that treating the past as fantasy acknowledges the IMPOSSIBILITY of recovering past world-views — the page says it acknowledges "the sort of difficulties James was referring to", and Kay expressly rejects James's impossibility thesis ("I don't agree, but I see the point")
verdict.trueWording: acknowledges the sort of difficulties James referred to — while disagreeing
verdict.note: Quote "a way of being honest about limitations" is verbatim on the page, and the Henry James framing is real: "It was Henry James who argued that historical fiction was, in fact, impossible ... getting to 'the real thing' with regard to the world views of people in the past simply could not be done." But Kay's own sentence is "I don't agree, but I see the point, and it strikes me forcibly that by treating the past through the form of a fantasy, one acknowledges the sort of difficulties James was referring to, while still probing and revealing motifs of the past." Difficulties acknowledged, impossibility disputed — so the claim's 'impossibility' limb overstates the source.

claim: Kay borrows Dunnett's method of demonstrating intelligence by having characters say things the reader does not get.
source: 'Guy Gavriel Kay: Margins of History', Locus (May 2025 excerpt) — read via Wayback copy
quote: say things the reader doesn’t understand

verdict.trueWording: Dunnett did this “by having him... say things the reader doesn’t understand”
verdict.note: Locus page reached raw (curl, HTTP 200). Quote is verbatim: “one of the ways she did it is by having him, or sometimes other people, say things the reader doesn’t understand.” But Kay presents this strictly as Dorothy Dunnett’s technique in the Lymond books, admired in the context of how hard it is “to convey the idea that a character is genuinely smart.” Nowhere on the page does he say he borrows or uses the device himself.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Kay borrows/adopts the method for his own fiction — the page attributes it to Dunnett only

claim: Walton remembers Arbonne chiefly through set-piece moments of the kind Kay does so well.
source: Jo Walton, 'Provencal Fantasy: Guy Gavriel Kay's A Song for Arbonne', Tor.com/Reactor (2010-08-06)
quote: a few set-piece moments, of the kind Kay does so well

verdict.trueWording: The characters, however, and the plot, had vanished from my mind ... except for a few set-piece moments
verdict.note: Quote is exact, but Walton's 'except' applies to characters and plot only — the same sentence-pair says 'I remembered the setting perfectly well' (lavender fields, Court of Love, troubadours), so set-pieces are not how she chiefly remembers the book.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that she remembers Arbonne chiefly through set-pieces — she remembered the setting perfectly well; only characters and plot had vanished

claim: Randall argues the reader must assemble Kay's secondary world by inference from the successive focalizations rather than from direct exposition.
quote: Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations.

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'rather than from direct exposition' - the page never contrasts focalization with exposition or direct description of the world
verdict.trueWording: "Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations."
verdict.note: Quotation is verbatim on the raw Randall page and the assembling-by-inference limb is supported ('Kay's forces us to experience Fionavar as its many characters do'; the strategy 'controls the speed and the manner in which we assimilate the culture of Fionavar'). But the article contains no occurrence of 'exposition' at all, and the only contrast it draws is with fantasies focalized through one or two central characters, not with expository delivery. The nearest support is a different sentence, about events rather than the world: 'the shifting is necessary if we are to observe the kernels directly, instead of having them related by direct speech or another kind of sub-narration.' Graded PARTIAL rather than verified because the contrastive limb is an inference the page does not state.

claim: Kay said in 1989 that if he rewrote The Fionavar Tapestry he would polish the prose of the opening chapters.
source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Raymond H. Thompson at Mythcon, Vancouver, 30 July 1989 (The Camelot Project, 1999)
quote: I might polish the prose itself
page: answer to 'If you could wave a magic wand that would rewrite the book'

verdict.trueWording: I might polish the prose itself, perhaps adding some gloss notes on character
verdict.note: Raw page (d.lib.rochester.edu Camelot Project, Raymond H. Thompson interview, Mythcon Vancouver, 30 July 1989) fetched via curl; quotation is verbatim. Date, work (the Fionavar trilogy - 'before the characters from our world cross to Fionavar'), and 'opening chapters' ('the first few chapters') all check out. The one limb the page does not carry is the flat 'would': Kay's definite 'would' attaches to paying attention to the first few chapters, while polishing the prose is explicitly hedged as 'I might'. Cure by rewording to 'said he might polish the prose'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the definite 'would polish' - the page says only 'I might polish the prose itself'
